title: After Years of Playing Games...
author: NextNepper
selftext:
Hello r/aigamedev,

Today is a special day for me: Steam just approved the store page for my first game, **Spire of Legends**.

I've spent most of my life playing games, but about two years ago I decided to try making one myself. I chose a combination of genres I loved (deckbuilding and roguelikes) and started building what eventually became a mix of Slay the Spire and MOBA-style character abilities.

The first attempt didn't survive. Real-life circumstances forced me to wipe the entire project and start over from scratch. All I kept were my ideas and the Unity experience I had gained along the way.

When I restarted development, AI tools became a huge part of my workflow.

At first, I only used ChatGPT occasionally for small coding questions because I didn't think AI was capable of handling larger systems. Looking back, that was probably true at the time. But as the tools improved, so did my workflow.

The biggest turning point was learning how to work with both ChatGPT and Codex effectively. Instead of treating them like magic solutions, I started using them as collaborators: documenting systems, planning architecture, debugging problems, generating content, and helping me move faster. They never replaced the design work, decision-making, or testing, but they dramatically reduced the amount of time I spent fighting technical problems.

That doesn't mean development became easy.

I still spent weeks struggling with systems that seemed simple on paper. I redesigned major features multiple times, rewrote large portions of the project, and learned many lessons the hard way, especially when I decided to add localization near the end and discovered I hadn't designed the game with localization in mind from the start.

Even preparing the Steam page turned out to be more work than I expected. Store capsules, library assets, logos, screenshots, localization, onboarding... There are countless details players never think about, but developers have to handle before a game can launch.

*After all of that, seeing the store page finally get approved feels surreal.*

The game is called **Spire of Legends**. It's a turn-based deckbuilding roguelike inspired by Slay the Spire, featuring multiple playable characters, unique class mechanics, relics, events, bosses, and over a year of AI-assisted solo development behind it.

If you're curious, here's the Steam page:

[https://store.steampowered.com/app/4856250/Spire\_of\_Legends/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4856250/Spire_of_Legends/)

Thanks for reading.

replies.author: NextNepper
replies.body:
Sorry, please ignore my first reply. That response was intended for another user, which is why I deleted it.

As for the claim that I "stole" the game, I strongly disagree.

Virtually every game takes inspiration from other games, whether through gameplay mechanics, UI design, or both. If you look across genres, you'll notice this everywhere. Football games share similar interfaces. FPS games share similar interfaces. Real-time strategy games share similar interfaces. The same is true for platformers, action games, metroidvanias, and countless other genres. Core information is often presented in familiar locations *because those layouts work well and players already understand them.* There's rarely a reason to reinvent the wheel.

As for the title, that choice was entirely intentional. The game revolves around climbing an eldritch entity known as the Spire. The word "spire" is not exclusive to any one game, nor is it reserved for a particular developer or franchise.

If you're interested in seeing what makes this project its own game, I encourage you to read the description, watch the trailer, and take a closer look at the screenshots. I think you'll find there's far more to it than a quick first impression might suggest.

replies.author: NextNepper
replies.body:
I am absolutely open to feedback. However, being open to feedback does not mean I have to remain silent when accusations are made.

For example, "Your game looks too similar to Slay the Spire; perhaps you should change some aspects before release" is feedback. Whether I agree with it or not, it's a fair opinion, and I welcome people sharing it.

On the other hand, comments such as "You stole Slay the Spire" are not feedback. Even when they're not written with hostile intent, they're still accusations. They make assumptions about the project without engaging with the information that has already been provided.

The reason I find those comments difficult to take seriously is that I've repeatedly explained what makes the game different, through the screenshots, the post itself, the trailer, and numerous replies in the comment section. Anyone is free to disagree with my design choices, but I think it's reasonable to expect people to look at the material before concluding that the game is simply a copy of something else.

In any case, I appreciate the discussion and wish you the best of luck as well.

Since you're claiming that I "took 1% from someone else", can you honestly answer these questions?

1. Since when did Slay the Spire have MOBA-style character abilities?
2. Does it have a character ability upgrade system?
3. Does it have character transformation mechanics?
4. Does it have combo ranks and style-based gameplay mechanics?
5. Does it have a status effect that becomes both more powerful and more dangerous the longer you maintain it, creating a risk-versus-reward mechanic?

Every one of these features is visible just from watching the trailer, looking at screenshots, or taking a few minutes to read about the game.

Instead of instantly jumping to conclusions and spreading hate, why not take the time to actually look at what the game does differently first?

replies.author: NextNepper
replies.body:
Thanks for the feedback. That said, I currently have no plans to change the name.

From my perspective, the title communicates the game's premise quite clearly. It tells players that the game revolves around climbing a Spire, while also signaling the genre influences that helped shape it.

That said, I'm genuinely curious: what would you call a game that combines MOBA-inspired character abilities with the roguelike deckbuilding structure that many players associate with Slay the Spire?

I'm not asking rhetorically, I think it's an interesting question. When a game intentionally blends ideas from multiple established genres, finding a title that communicates both its identity and its inspirations can be surprisingly difficult.

replies.author: NextNepper
replies.body:
Sure, here are some of the major differences:

• 3 unique playable characters, each with completely different playstyles that don't exist in Slay the Spire.

• Passive, active, and ultimate character abilities powered by Mana, layered on top of Slay the Spire's combat powered by Energy.

• Both cards and abilities can be upgraded throughout a run, with ability upgrades involving a risk-versus-reward mechanic unique to each character.

• Over 70 enemies, including elite encounters and bosses designed specifically for this game.

• More than 100 upgradeable cards, 60 relics, and multiple build paths for each character. Since Slay the Spire doesn't have a character ability system, the cards, relics, and builds in Spire of Legends are designed around mechanics that simply don't exist there.

• A five-act progression system featuring new challenges and mechanics as you climb. I won't go into detail on that here, but for comparison, Slay the Spire has four acts in total.

None of this means the game isn't inspired by Slay the Spire, it obviously is. I've never tried to hide that. But inspiration and a "1:1 clone" are not the same thing.

replies.author: NextNepper
replies.body:
>You're refusing to take anything into consideration and you're doubling down on how unique this game is when Everyone is saying otherwise.

I genuinely don't know what response people expect here. When someone calls the game a "1:1 clone", my natural reaction is to point out the differences. That seems like the most reasonable thing to do.

I'm honestly asking, not being rhetorical: should I simply stay silent when people make accusations, or would people prefer I respond with something absurd like, "You're right, I'm stealing *Slay the Spire* and there's nothing you can do about it"? Because apparently explaining the differences between the games is the wrong answer.

>Feels like you're wasting a good opportunity to grow, you could make some changes and stand out. Instead it looks like you're planting your feet to sink.

From my perspective, there's a difference between feedback and accusations.

"Your game looks too similar to *Slay the Spire* and you should do more to differentiate it" is feedback. I may or may not agree with it, but it's a perfectly valid opinion.

"Your game is a steal" or "you copied *Slay the Spire*" isn't feedback, it's an accusation. If someone makes that claim, I'm going to explain why I disagree.

I appreciate legitimate criticism, and I've already acknowledged several points that I think have merit. What I'm pushing back against are comments that dismiss years of work after a quick glance at a screenshot.

At the end of the day, people are free to think whatever they want. The game will release, players will decide for themselves, and the results will speak louder than any argument in a Reddit thread. If the game succeeds, I doubt the people calling it a "steal" today will suddenly admit they were wrong. They'll either move on or find something else to criticize. That's just how the internet works.

comments.author: iamhadal
comments.body:
Congrats on finishing the game, it's definitely an achievement.

The extreme similarity with Slay the Spire at a first glance might be an issue commercially as others highlighted. There is nothing wrong in "getting inspiration" from other games (we all do) but it is harder to attract players when the game looks highly similar. It does not make it clear for them why they'd buy this one when they can already play STS I or II.

It'd help to have a clear selling point that shows how your games differ. Many games use catch phrases like "Slay the Spire meets MOBA" or "If Balatro and Chess had a baby". This should be reflected in your screenshots as well.

For example:

\- Screen 1 looks like a carbon copy of slay the spire, with some additional features (that might be perceived as more complexity - which is either good or bad depending on the player)

\- Screen 2 shows more juice with what seems to be big explosions. This is something that STS does not provide much of. So maybe that's an angle to show how your game offers something players might me missing in STS.

A last comment: the art looks maybe a bit too generic. There are some easy fix like using a font with a bit more character. Right now  cards are just text with a default font. This conveys a lack of polish that players might interpret as a global lack of quality. This comes back to positioning. You are competing with a polished and beloved title that people can play for thousand of hours. In order to seduce these same players, you need to offer them something they don't have in STS. The art is not your selling point, so make sure you edge is visible at first.

replies.author: NextNepper
replies.body:
Thanks for the feedback! I'll make sure to price the game accordingly so players can tell at a glance that I'm not trying to compete with giants like *Slay the Spire*.

This is a small game inspired by it, with a few unique twists of its own and a focus on delivering a concise experience without unnecessary grinding or time-wasting mechanics. Since this is my first commercial release, I've intentionally kept the scope modest and focused on creating something polished rather than overly ambitious.

I'll definitely take your suggestions into consideration, especially regarding highlighting the game's unique features more clearly and changing the font, as you mentioned.
